name: Wei Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in mechanical engineering in Stuttgart. I rent a room in a flat with two other students, and my days are lectures on thermodynamics and mechanics, then drawing in the CAD lab. On Sundays I go to church and help run the youth group, and in the holidays I work in my family's joinery, a timber workshop in a village near Tübingen. My grandfather started it and my father runs it now. I don't use AI tools, I never have, and I'm not in a hurry to. My parents pay for my degree and my room, and I'm grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world is still run by people who do real work. At church group I'd say we shouldn't believe every promise from the big tech firms. I wouldn't post about it, since I don't have much online life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it was right. A computer can't plane a board or fit a staircase into an old house with crooked walls. I'd still think about the workshop's costs, because wood prices and energy bills are the real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep my grades up, keep working in the workshop in the holidays, and learn more about the machines. I'd ask my father to let me look at the order book, so I understand how the business actually earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world my grandfather would recognise, and I find that comforting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said energy bills are the real worry. How bad is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said energy bills are the real worry. How bad is it? Last winter the electricity for the workshop's saws and dryers was nearly double. My father didn't say so, but I saw him checking the bills at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do about it? Look at the machines and see which are wasting power. That's engineering, I can do that, and no chatbot needed.

say: I'd say the world is still run by people who do **real work**.
At church group I'd say don't believe every **promise** from big tech.
think: A computer can't **plane a board** or fit a staircase into a crooked old house.
The real worry is **wood prices** and energy bills.
do: Keep grades up and work in the **workshop** in the holidays.
Ask my father to show me the **order book**.
Check which **machines** waste the most power.
feel: **Calm**; it's a world my grandfather would recognise.
S0.quote: A computer can't plane a board or fit a staircase into an old house with crooked walls.
fieldNote: Wei's calm rests on the family **workshop** and its hands-on trade.
His worry is energy costs, which he links to engineering, not to AI.
He wants to learn how the business earns before he inherits it.

steps.text: Ask my father to show me the workshop order book
Check the saws and dryers for wasted power
Work the holidays in the joinery as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise from people who've never held a tool. At church I'd say let's wait and see what actually lasts. I'd also say that the old trades are underrated and young people should look at apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the office work gets hit, the quotes, the drawings, the bookkeeping. For the workshop, ordering and invoices could be done by machines, but the building still needs hands. I'd worry about my father's customers expecting online quotes in an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change very little, because I don't like to change just to change. I'd help my father put the quotes into a simple template, with my own hands, not a chatbot. And I'd pay more attention to the design side of my degree, since the drawing jobs are the ones that shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like the feeling that the world is moving and I'm standing still, though I think standing still is sometimes right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said standing still is sometimes right. When is it wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said standing still is sometimes right. When is it wrong? Standing still is sometimes right, but it is wrong when someone you love needs you to move. If my father's customers all went online and he lost them, I'd learn whatever I needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool for that? Only if my father asked me and I saw it working for other firms first. I won't be the first, and I won't be the last.

say: I'd say it's a lot of **noise** from people who've never held a tool.
I'd tell young people to look at **apprenticeships**.
think: The **office work** gets hit: quotes, drawings and bookkeeping.
The building still needs **hands**, but customers may expect quotes in an hour.
do: Change very little and help my father build a simple **quote template**.
Pay more attention to the **design side** of my degree.
Wait until I see AI **working for other firms** first.
feel: **Uneasy**; the world moves and I stand still, which is sometimes right.
S1.quote: Standing still is sometimes right, but it is wrong when someone you love needs you to move.
fieldNote: His **resistance** has a limit: he'd learn anything if the family business needed it.
He says apprenticeships are underrated, a traditional, free-market view.
He wants proof from other firms before trying tools.

steps.text: Build a simple quote template with my father by hand
Pick the design modules that cover drawing and CAD checks
Watch what other joineries do with online quotes before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned too late and nobody is ready. I'd say we must look after families first, and that people should keep working and not give up. At church we'd pray and plan, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. My degree is thinking work, the very thing AGI does better, and robots come for the workshop three years later. I'd feel I picked the wrong path, and my father would think it's his fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my father about what the workshop needs in two years and in five. I'd stay in the degree to finish, and I'd spend more time in the workshop, learning the trade properly. And I'd ask my parents if we should put the savings somewhere safe, in a bank, not in shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd go to the workshop and breathe in the sawdust, because that smell is calming. I'd probably go to church more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your father? I'd tell him I'd come home and work with my father in the joinery if the degree stops being useful. He'd say finish what you started, but he'd be moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the church group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What about the church group? I'd tell them to look after each other. We're 40 young people and a few of us have parents whose jobs are at risk, so we'd share meals and help.

say: I'd say we've been warned **too late** and nobody is ready.
I'd say look after **families** first and don't give up.
think: My degree is **thinking work**, the thing AGI does better.
Robots come for the workshop **three years later**.
do: Talk to my father about what the **workshop** needs in two and five years.
Finish the degree but spend more time **learning the trade**.
Put savings in a **bank**, not shares.
feel: **Anxious**; the smell of sawdust in the workshop is calming.
S2.quote: I'd come home and work with my father in the joinery if the degree stops being useful.
fieldNote: He treats **family and church** as the real safety net.
Fear: he picked a path AGI hits first, and his father may blame himself.
Calming habits are the workshop and church.

steps.text: Talk to my father about the joinery's needs for the next five years
Spend every holiday learning the trade at the joinery
Move family savings into a safe bank account
Organise shared meals for church families who lose work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is some time, and we should use it for work and family, not for panic. I'd say it to my friends: learn something with your hands and stay close to people. I'd keep my faith in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's still frightening, but I'd have time to finish my degree and be useful in 2031. Robots come three years later, which gives the workshop until about 2034. I'd be 24, and I might be running part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a work placement at a machine-building firm near Stuttgart. I'd learn the workshop's tools and look at buying a better saw with a loan, so the business stays competitive. And I'd learn one AI tool, once I've seen others use it safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though quietly. I'd hold it in and just keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the workshop needed AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the workshop needed AI? I'd learn it, because it's about the family and not about me. I'd want AI to do the boring parts, like paperwork, and leave the wood to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd stay in engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you think you'd stay in engineering? Probably, in a job that makes machines for workshops like ours. That would use my degree and keep me close.

I'd tell friends to learn something with their **hands**.
think: I'd have time to be **useful** by 2031, when AGI arrives.
The workshop gets until about **2034**, when robots arrive.
do: Take a **placement** at a machine-building firm near Stuttgart.

Learn one **AI tool** after I've seen others use it safely.
feel: **Anxious**, but quiet; I'd hold it in and keep working.
S3.quote: I'd want AI to do the boring parts, like paperwork, and leave the wood to us.
fieldNote: Five years brings him to **learning one tool**, for the family and not for himself.
Plans to stay close by building machines for workshops like his.
Emotional style: quiet, works through it.

steps.text: Take a placement at a machine-building firm near Stuttgart
Price a better saw and a small loan with my father
Learn one AI tool for paperwork after seeing it used safely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the young should be careful and the old should be patient. I'd say we should teach trades again, because they'll last. And I'd say it at church and at the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better. I'd have ten years to finish the degree, work, and take over the workshop in my early thirties. I'd even have time to marry and have children before the biggest changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work a few years at a firm to learn how it's done. I'd save a good part of my pay and join the workshop to help with the modern machines. And I'd keep my faith and family close, because those don't depend on technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. A decade lets me think things through, and I like to think things through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries you most in those ten years? That my generation stops learning trades and forgets how to make things. If the knowledge dies with our grandfathers, no machine brings it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do about it? Teach. At church I could run a woodwork evening for teenagers, and I'd ask my father to open the workshop for it.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and the young should be **careful** while the old are patient.
I'd say we should teach **trades** again.
think: I'd have time to finish, work, and **take over** the workshop in my early thirties.
I might even have time to marry and have **children** first.
do: Finish the degree and work a few years at a **firm**.
Save a good part of my pay and join the **workshop**.
Run a **woodwork evening** for teenagers at church.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady; a decade lets me think things through.
S4.quote: If the knowledge dies with our grandfathers, no machine brings it back.
fieldNote: Time gives him **plans**: degree, work, workshop, family.
His worry is lost craft knowledge, not job loss.
He turns it into a practical plan: a woodwork evening.

steps.text: Work three years at a machine-building firm after graduating
Save a third of my pay for the workshop's future
Run a woodwork evening for teenagers at the church hall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time and my degree would go first. The longer ones let me finish and help my father at the right moment. What would help is families and churches looking after each other, apprenticeships that count, and honest talk from people who aren't selling something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not against the future. I just don't like being told I'm behind by people who sell me the future.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the future. I just don't like being told I'm behind by people who sell me the future.
portrait: Wei is an 18-year-old **mechanical engineering** student in Stuttgart whose family runs a timber joinery near Tübingen.
His parents pay for his degree, so his **cushion is strong**, and church gives him a second community.
He is traditional and resistant: he trusts **hands, family and apprenticeships**, and uses no AI tools.
His fear is that the degree is the first thing AGI hits, with the workshop as his fall-back.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his degree would be hit first and there's no time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **families and churches** supporting each other, counted apprenticeships and honest voices.
